newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain 1997 deficit seen on track after March data.
newsitem.headline: Spain 1997 deficit seen on track after March data.

text.p: Spain delivered a bloated first quarter state budget deficit of 836 billion pesetas, on a national account basis, on Wednesday but analysts said Spain would still reach its 1997 target.

Spain brought foward payments and delayed revenues, making it impossible to translate what look like bad figures -- in only three months the state had already run up almost half of its planned two trillion peseta deficit -- into a gloomy forecast.

"I am confident that they will end as they forecast mainly for two reasons: a sustained economic growth at around 5.25 percent in nominal terms and the reduction in yields," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.

Earlier on Wednesday Spain announced a budget deficit for the first three months on a cash basis of 861.2 billion versus 200.3 billion pesetas in the first two months this year and up from 628.1 billion pesetas in the first quarter 1996.
But on a national account basis the first quarter showed a deficit at 836 billion pesetas, down 30.1 percent.

Economy Secretary Jose Folgado, when presenting the data, reiterated that Spain was on track to meet its 1997 deficit to gross domestic product ratio goal of 2.5 percent, despite the fact that the first quarter value stood at 1.1 percent.

"You can't multiple the deficit/gdp percentage we had in the first quarter by four...because total expenditures won't be the expenditures we had by four, and revenues won't be the revenues we had by four," Folgado said.
But some analysts said revenues remained low.

"It seems revenues did better than we were expecting, but they are still low. If the government wants to meet the target, keeping the expenditures in line with the budget, it needs cash of around 16 trillion pesetas coming in," said Alfonso Novales of the independent research group Eriste in Madrid.
"If the trend we had in March continues, total revenues will be at around 15.65 trillion, with a 355 million peseta gap."
First quarter revenues were 3.978 trillion pesetas, up 14.9 percent from the same period a year ago.
"These figures are better than what we had in the first two months, but it's still too early to say they are in line," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at Bank of America.
Particularly on the expenditures side the government had anticipated many payments.
Folgado said that in the first quarter alone, the state had given back more than half of the total amount of taxes it was refunding to firms.
Also interest payments, up 24.4 percent from the previous year, are set to decline in the coming months. The government has said they will rise a modest two percent over the full 1997.
Money transfers from the state jumped 18.8 percent, with a big rise in anticipated money to regional governments -- up 29.3 percent -- and to the European Community -- up 42.4 percent.
The March deficit raised analysts' eyebrows, but they said it was really too early to conclude that Spain would need to take additional measures to keep its budget on track.

"In April or May these figures will give as a better idea. The 30 percent fall in the deficit on a national account basis is very good, but still we have so many months yet," said Heather Richardson at UBS in London.
